guide.summary: Team, Transform, and Transmit covers collaboration, turning research into solutions, communicating to specific audiences through written and multimedia presentations, defending your work orally, and reflecting on your process.

sections.heading: Teamwork
sections.body: Effective teams divide research by lens or subtopic so that members bring different perspectives, set shared goals and deadlines, and meet regularly to integrate findings. Productive collaboration means listening, giving and receiving specific feedback, resolving disagreements by returning to evidence and shared goals, and holding everyone accountable. A team's final argument should be integrated, not a sequence of separate mini-presentations: the economic, health, policy, and community findings in the food-access scenario should combine into one explanation of the problem and one well-supported solution, with trade-offs acknowledged.

sections.heading: Transforming research into solutions and presentations
sections.body: Solutions should follow from the evidence and be feasible, considering cost, stakeholders, and unintended consequences. Compare alternatives (for example, tax incentives to attract a grocery store vs supporting a cooperative market vs mobile produce markets) and justify the choice. Tailor communication to the audience: city council members care about cost, legal authority, and constituents, so lead with the problem's scale, a specific proposal, and its budget implications. Multimedia should support the spoken argument: one idea per slide, clear data visualizations with labeled axes and sources, minimal text, and visuals that clarify rather than decorate. Delivery matters: eye contact, a clear voice, purposeful pacing, and not reading from slides.

sections.heading: Oral defense and reflection
sections.body: In the oral defense, you answer questions about your research process and argument: why you chose a lens or source, how you handled conflicting evidence, what you would do differently, and how your thinking changed. Strong answers are specific (naming sources, decisions, and reasons), honest about limitations, and connect back to the argument. Reflection is metacognition about your process: what worked, what didn't, how collaboration shaped the outcome, and how you would improve. Admitting a limitation, such as a small interview sample, and explaining how you addressed it shows mastery rather than weakness.

sections.heading: Worked example: an oral defense answer
sections.body: A panelist asks, 'Why did you choose to focus on cooperative grocery stores rather than tax incentives for chains?' A weak answer says, 'Because I liked that idea better.' A strong answer explains the evidence and reasoning: 'Our economic research showed that chain stores often close underperforming locations because of thin margins, and our interviews showed residents wanted local ownership. We compared both options on cost, sustainability, and community support, and the cooperative scored better on two of three criteria, though it requires more startup support.' The strong answer is specific, references research, and acknowledges a limitation.

sections.heading: Team challenges and solutions
sections.body: Common team problems include uneven workloads, missed deadlines, and disagreements about the argument. Solutions include assigning clear roles, setting shared deadlines with check-ins, keeping notes in a shared document, and resolving disagreements by returning to the evidence and the team's goals. Teams should also integrate findings throughout the project rather than combining separate pieces at the end, which often produces a disconnected presentation.

sections.heading: Presentation delivery
sections.body: Rehearse transitions between speakers so the presentation flows as one argument. Speak to the audience rather than reading slides, use visuals that show evidence clearly, and time the presentation to fit the limit. Prepare for questions by anticipating weaknesses in your research and practicing honest, specific answers.

sections.heading: Going deeper
sections.body: Reflection is ongoing, not just at the end. Throughout the project, note what is working in your team, what problems arise, and how you respond. These notes make your oral defense answers specific and honest. Strong reflection identifies a concrete lesson and explains how you would apply it next time, such as agreeing on a research question earlier, setting clearer deadlines, or gathering more diverse sources. Readers and panelists value self-awareness and growth.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know audience, feasibility, trade-off, unintended consequence, multimedia, delivery, oral defense, and reflection. Strong presentations combine a clear argument, evidence-based visuals, and confident delivery, and strong oral defenses give specific, honest answers about the research process.

keyTakeaways: Divide work by lens, then integrate findings.
Resolve conflict with evidence and shared goals.
Solutions must be feasible and justified against alternatives.
Tailor the message to the audience.
Oral defense answers are specific and honest.
commonMistakes: Proposing solutions the evidence doesn't support.
Defensive or vague oral defense answers.
examTips: Practice answering 'Why did you choose this source?' and 'What would you change?' with specifics.
Rehearse transitions between team members so the argument flows.
guide.cramSheet:
**Team:** divide by lens · deadlines · integrate · feedback · resolve by evidence

**Solution:** evidence-based · feasible · stakeholders · alternatives · trade-offs

**Presentation:** audience-tailored · one idea per slide · labeled visuals · cite sources · eye contact

**Oral defense:** specific · honest about limits · link to argument

**Reflection:** what worked · what didn't · what you'd change

practice.stimulus:
Practice scenario (written by Klutch)

A four-person team is researching why many residents of a low-income neighborhood lack easy access to fresh food. Each member investigates a different lens: economic (grocery store profit margins), health (diet-related illness rates), policy (zoning and tax incentives), and community (residents' own priorities, from interviews). The team must produce a multimedia presentation proposing a solution to an audience of city council members, and each member will answer oral defense questions.
practice.stem: Why should team members research different lenses?

choices.text: So each member can present an unrelated topic
To bring multiple perspectives and evidence types that strengthen the team's analysis
To avoid having to communicate
Because College Board assigns lenses

practice.explanation: Diverse lenses reveal more of a complex problem.

practice.stem: Which slide practice best supports an oral argument?

choices.text: Every statistic from the research on one slide
Paragraphs of text read aloud
Decorative images unrelated to the point
A labeled chart with a cited source and a short headline stating its takeaway

practice.explanation: Visuals should clarify the spoken argument.

practice.prompt: Using the scenario, propose a solution to the city council.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: State your solution and the evidence from at least two lenses that supports it.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Compare it with an alternative and justify your choice.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Identify a trade-off or unintended consequence and how to address it.

rubric.description: A specific, evidence-based proposal that integrates at least two lenses.
Compares it with at least one alternative and justifies the choice.
Identifies a cost or unintended consequence and how to mitigate it.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. We propose that the city fund a community-owned cooperative grocery with a five-year startup grant and lease a city-owned lot at low cost. Our health research showed high diet-related illness rates, our community interviews showed residents want local ownership, and our policy research found that zoning on the city-owned lot already allows retail.

B. A tax incentive for a chain store could open faster, but our economic research showed thin grocery margins lead chains to close underperforming stores, and residents preferred local control. The cooperative better fits both the evidence and community priorities.

C. A cooperative may struggle financially at first. To reduce this risk, the grant could be tied to benchmarks, and the city could partner with an established cooperative network for management training.

practice.prompt: Answer these oral defense questions as the community-lens researcher on the team.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Why did you choose your research method, and how did you carry it out?

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: What was a limitation of your research, and how did you address it?

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: How did your thinking change during the project, and what would you do differently?

rubric.description: Honestly identifies a limitation and how it was addressed.
Explains how thinking changed or what would be done differently, with reasons.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. I chose interviews because census data told us how far residents live from stores but not why they shop where they do or what they'd want instead. I recruited participants through a neighborhood association and a church to reach residents of different ages.

B. With only 12 interviews, my sample can't represent everyone, and I likely reached more engaged residents. I addressed this by comparing what I heard with a city survey on shopping habits, which matched the main themes.

C. I began assuming the problem was distance, but interviews showed price and store hours mattered just as much. Next time I'd add a short survey to reach more residents and test that finding.

practice.prompt: A teammate's draft slide reads: 'FOOD DESERTS' as a title, followed by eight bullet points of full sentences and a stock photo of vegetables.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how the presenter should deliver it to the council.

rubric.description: Identifies problems: too much text, vague title, decorative image, no data or source.
Describes a redesign with a takeaway headline, a single visual, and a source.
Explains how the speaker should present it to the council.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. The slide has too much text, so the audience will read instead of listening; the title names a topic instead of a takeaway; and the stock photo adds nothing. It also has no data or sources.

B. Redesign: headline 'One in three residents lives over a mile from a full grocery store,' a map showing store locations and the neighborhood, and a small source citation.

C. The speaker should state the takeaway, point to the gap on the map, explain one consequence (higher diet-related illness), and transition to the proposal, speaking to council members rather than reading.

practice.prompt: Write a reflection on a collaborative project (real or this scenario).

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain why one part of the process worked or did not.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Describe a specific change you would make next time.

rubric.description: Describes specific actions and decisions, not generalities.
Explains why something worked or failed.
Identifies a concrete change for future work.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Our team divided research by lens and met twice a week. In the first two weeks, we each worked separately and our draft was four disconnected sections.

B. This failed because we never agreed on a shared research question; each member chased their own. Once we wrote a single question, 'What is the most feasible way to improve fresh food access in this neighborhood?', our findings started to connect.

C. In future projects, I'll push the team to agree on the research question and evaluation criteria in the first meeting, and to share summaries of findings weekly so integration happens throughout rather than at the end.
